newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu to seek no-violence pledge at summit.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu to seek no-violence pledge at summit.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu hopes to win a commitment from Palestinian President Yasser Arafat at a Washington meeting this week to remove violence as an option in the making of Middle East peace.

But the right-wing Israeli leader said he had no plans to close a controversial Jerusalem tunnel, the opening of which enraged Palestinians and sparked four days of Arab-Israeli violence that claimed 69 lives.

"We can first of all bring a new vitality, a new commitment to the peace process," Netanyahu told CNN on Sunday after he accepted an invitation from U.S. President Bill Clinton to meet Arafat in Washington.
"In practical effect, I think we should achieve two principles: one, an immediate and permanent cessation of violence and hostilities and two, an accelerated return to negotiations," he said.

Israel's opening of the tunnel near Moslem holy sites in Jerusalem, whose final status is hotly disputed between Israelis and Arabs, combined with festering Palestinian frustration over Netanyahu's policies to ignite last week's clashes.
Netanyahu has accused Arafat of instigating the violence, which has since died down, to pressure his right-wing government into making peace concessions.
Palestinians say they are fed up by what they describe as Netanyahu's foot-dragging in implementing peace deals, especially Israel's promised troop redeployment in the West Bank city of Hebron.
Asked if he would close the tunnel, Netanyahu told CNN: "I don't know. Would you tear down the Washington monument or stop the Vietnam Memorial if somebody says they have a problem with it?"
The tunnel, he added, is "not on my table and it won't be on my table."

Clinton said both Netanyahu and Arafat had accepted his invitation, but a Palestinian official said Arafat was insisting that Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak must also attend the talks, tentatively scheduled for Tuesday and Wednesday..

A White House spokesman confirmed that Clinton had spoken to Arafat, Netanyahu, King Hussein of Jordan and Mubarak, adding that the United States "fully expects" Arafat to come to Washington, regardless of Mubarak's presence.

Netanyahu was due to leave for the United States on Monday. The Palestinian official said Arafat would go to Cairo to try to persuade Mubarak, who has waged a war of words with Israel over the slow pace of peace, to attend the Washington meeting.

Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa told CBS television that Mubarak wanted some assurance that Israel would honour its past agreements with the Palestinians before agreeing to take part in the talks.

Asked why Netanyahu and Arafat were now willing to meet, Clinton said: "I think that they're both concerned about the way that events have spun out of control, about the loss of life, the injury, the eruption of old tensions and bitterness.
"And I believe they want to try to get beyond that and go back to moving toward the path of peace. I don't think they would be coming here if they didn't."
